items.followUp: Why does sweating cool the body?

rubric.why: The faster, higher-energy molecules preferentially escape from the liquid during evaporation.
rubric.description: Identifies the molecules that escape during evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that faster or higher-energy molecules escape.

rubric.why: The remaining liquid has lower average kinetic energy or absorbs heat from its surroundings, so it cools.
rubric.description: Explains why the remaining liquid cools.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the loss of energy or heat absorption to cooling.

modelAnswer: During evaporation, the higher-energy molecules escape from the surface of the liquid.
The average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules decreases, so the liquid absorbs heat from its surroundings and cools.
Thus, evaporation is a cooling process.
A similar example is the cooling effect of sweat evaporating from the skin.

items.followUp: State the Bohr postulates that explain the emission of a spectral line.

rubric.why: Bohr proposed that electrons occupy permitted orbits, each with a definite energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons occupy permitted orbits or energy levels with definite energies.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for identifying the permitted orbits and their definite energies.

rubric.why: An electron in a permitted orbit does not continuously radiate or lose energy.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while in a permitted orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an electron does not radiate or lose energy while remaining in an orbit.

rubric.why: An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher level and emits energy when it moves to a lower level.
rubric.description: Describes energy absorption or emission during a transition between levels.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly relating absorption to an upward transition or emission to a downward transition.

rubric.why: The absorbed or emitted energy equals the difference between the two energy levels.
rubric.description: States the energy relationship for a transition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving ΔE = hν or an equivalent statement that the energy equals the difference between levels.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain permitted circular orbits called energy levels or shells.
Each permitted orbit has a definite energy.
An electron does not radiate energy while it remains in a permitted orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher energy level and emits energy when it moves to a lower energy level.
The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the two energy levels: ΔE = hν.

items.followUp: Explain why water molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding involves hydrogen covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom, commonly N, O, or F.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating that hydrogen is covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F.

rubric.why: The hydrogen is attracted to a lone pair or partial negative charge on an electronegative atom in a nearby molecule.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for describing the attraction between hydrogen and a nearby electronegative atom or its lone pair.

rubric.why: Water is a relevant example of molecules that form hydrogen bonds.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of hydrogen bonding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving water as an example.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is an intermolecular electrostatic attraction involving a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as N, O, or F.
The hydrogen atom is attracted to a lone pair or partial negative charge on an electronegative atom in a nearby molecule.
For example, hydrogen bonds form between neighbouring water (H₂O) molecules.
Hydrogen bonding is weaker than a covalent bond.
